disease_notes: Moderately resistant to peach leaf curl; moderately susceptible to bacterial spot; resistant to leaf spot
variety_notes: Released by Michigan State University in 1940 (Dr. Stanley Johnston). Set the standard for freestone peaches. Vigorous grower that requires yearly thinning. Often planted as pollinator partner for other peaches even though self-fertile. Yields 50-100+ lbs on a mature tree.
sources: Cummins Nursery; TreeCareZone; Monrovia; Food Forest Nursery; Stark Bros; One Green World; NatureHills
source_notes: Zone range: most sources say 4-8; TreeCareZone and Food Forest Nursery list 5-9. Used 4-8 as the more conservative cold-end.

disease_notes: Good disease resistance; resistant to brown rot
variety_notes: Classic American heirloom from the 1870s. Large golden-yellow freestone peach with red blush. Perfect for fresh eating, baking, canning, and preserves. Heavy cropper requiring thinning for fruit size.
sources: Stark Bros; Bates Nursery; Food Forest Nursery; Gardening Know How; Plant Me Green; Talbott Nursery; Epic Gardening
source_notes: Chill hours commonly cited at 800-950 (some sources say 600-950 for Early Elberta); zone range typically 5-8 but Gardening Know How extends to 9.

disease_notes: Tolerant to peach leaf curl; standard peach pest/disease concerns otherwise
variety_notes: Bred at University of New Hampshire in 1964 by Professor Meader specifically for cold-climate growing. Often called the most cold-hardy peach, hardy to approximately -25F. Flower buds especially hardy. Medium-to-large red-blushed yellow freestone. Fruit quality is rated good rather than great but reliability in harsh climates is unmatched. Mid-August in Southeast Wisconsin.
sources: Stark Bros; Raintree Nursery; Grandpa's Orchard; Gardenia; Johnson's Nursery; Practical Self Reliance; Restoring Eden; Fast Growing Trees
source_notes: Chill hours range 1000-1050 across most sources. Practical Self Reliance notes Contender is often preferred over Reliance for fruit quality where both will grow.

disease_notes: Excellent resistance to bacterial spot; susceptible to peach leaf curl
variety_notes: Released by NC State University in 1988. Received the American Society for Horticultural Science Outstanding Fruit Cultivar Award in 2014. The high chill requirement causes late bloom which reliably escapes spring frosts — a major advantage in zones 5-6. Large red-over-yellow freestone with yellow flesh and excellent aromatic flavor. Hardy to -40F per One Green World. Considered the best-quality cold-hardy peach.
sources: Stark Bros; Cummins Nursery; Raintree Nursery; Johnson's Nursery; One Green World; Gurney's; Plant Me Green; Food Forest Nursery; Roots to Fruits
source_notes: All sources strongly agree on fundamentals.

disease_notes: Moderately resistant to peach leaf curl; moderately resistant to brown rot
variety_notes: Released by Texas A&M in 1965. Parentage: July (Kim) Elberta x Floriberta. Medium-sized yellow freestone with small pit. Low chill requirement makes it excellent for southern states and areas with warm winters. Ripens 15 days before Elberta. Named for Sam Houston, first president of the Republic of Texas. Heavy producer — requires aggressive thinning in April.
sources: Dave Wilson Nursery; Texas Pecan Nursery; Willis Orchards; Urban Harvest; Texas Tree Farms; Yarden; Legg Creek Farm; Food Forest Nursery
source_notes: Zone range 5-8 per Dave Wilson; some low-chill sources extend to zone 9. Plant Me Green lists 7-9 as a warmer-climate preference.

disease_notes: Moderately resistant to bacterial spot; standard peach pest/disease concerns
variety_notes: Released by Texas A&M from the Prairie View, Texas breeding program. Semi-freestone, medium-sized yellow peach with red blush. Excellent fresh eating and canning. Moderate chill requirement makes it versatile across middle zones.
sources: Dave Wilson Nursery; Texas Pecan Nursery; Stark Bros
source_notes: Slightly less-documented than some varieties; pulled from consistent nursery catalog data. Chill hours commonly cited at 750-800.

disease_notes: Good tolerance to bacterial spot and brown rot
variety_notes: Released by Virginia Agricultural Experiment Station in 1963. Known for exceptional late frost tolerance and cold hardiness — excels in marginal peach areas. Medium-large freestone peach with bright red blush over orange skin. Minimally fibrous orange-yellow flesh. Heavy producer requiring thinning.
sources: Grandpa's Orchard; Mehrabyan Nursery; 13 Point 3 Farms; Stark Bros
source_notes: Frost tolerance is the standout attribute. Zone range widely cited as 4-8.

disease_notes: Resistant to leaf spot; bacterial spot resistance
variety_notes: Released in 1963 by Michigan State University (South Haven). Large golden-yellow freestone with bright red blush and almost fuzzless skin. Firm yellow flesh resists browning — excellent for canning and freezing. Late bloom helps avoid spring frosts. Consistently well-reviewed for flavor and reliability.
sources: Stark Bros; Food Forest Nursery; Mehrabyan Nursery; Tomorrow's Harvest; Plant Me Green; NC State Extension
source_notes: Chill hours range 750-1000 across sources; used 800-950 as the consensus.

disease_notes: Resistant to bacterial spot; fruit resists browning
variety_notes: Released from Michigan State University. Large, round, uniform freestone with attractive red mottling over yellow background. Flavorful yellow flesh is fuzzless and non-browning — excellent for canning. Grows well in western and midwestern states. Hangs well on the tree.
sources: Stark Bros; Blue Hill Wildlife Nursery; Roots to Fruits Nursery
source_notes: Less documented than some varieties but consistent data where available.

disease_notes: Slightly susceptible to bacterial spot; moderately resistant to brown rot
variety_notes: Released by USDA in 1969 from Fresno, California. Parentage: Gold King x open-pollinated seedling of Red King. Large bright-red freestone with yellow flesh. Firm, juicy, tangy flavor — continues to sweeten when allowed to ripen on tree. One of the benchmark yellow-fleshed nectarines. Excellent adaptability across zones 5-9.
sources: Cummins Nursery; Food Forest Nursery; Stark Bros; NatureHills; Epic Gardening; Bay Laurel Nursery
source_notes: Chill hours: Cummins cites 500; Food Forest 500-600; Epic Gardening notes as low as 250 for some sources. Used 500-600 as consensus.

disease_notes: Valued for resistance to brown rot and leaf spot
variety_notes: Introduced in the 1950s in New Hampshire. One of the hardiest nectarines available — withstands temperatures as low as -28F. Freestone with rich sweet-tangy flavor that rivals warm-climate nectarines. Proven performer for 70+ years in cold climates.
sources: Stark Bros; Bay Laurel Nursery; Epic Gardening
source_notes: Chill hours 950 per Stark Bros.

disease_notes: Excellent resistance to bacterial spot and brown rot; note: susceptible to peach leaf curl in wet-spring climates (e.g., Pacific Northwest)
variety_notes: Released from Harrow Research Station, Ontario, Canada in 1974. Hardy to -20F or below. Semi-freestone with firm yellow flavorful flesh. One of the most disease-resistant nectarines — especially good for low-spray growing. Large showy pink flowers. Adapted to cooler climates.
sources: Stark Bros; Raintree Nursery; One Green World; NatureHills; Intermountain Fruit
source_notes: Chill hours: Raintree cites 800+, Intermountain Fruit notes low chilling, One Green World hardy to -20F. Zone range 4-9 per One Green World. Hardy for northern climates but has peach leaf curl issues in Pacific Northwest.

disease_notes: Crack-resistant; good shelf life; buds are hardy
variety_notes: Large freestone with red-gold skin and rich flavorful yellow flesh. Great for baking and fresh eating. Productive tree with beautiful pink flowers in spring. Crack-resistant fruit with good shelf life. Buds hardy to -20F.
sources: Stark Bros; Talbott Nursery; Intermountain Fruit; NatureHills
source_notes: Chill hours 850 per Talbott Nursery.

disease_notes: Standard nectarine pest/disease concerns
variety_notes: White-fleshed nectarine bred by the Zaiger family of California — part of the Arctic series. Very low chill requirement (lowest of the Arctic series). Rich, sweet flavor. Excellent for mild-winter climates. Earliest-ripening of the Arctic whites (mid-to-late June).
sources: Stark Bros; Bay Laurel Nursery; NatureHills
source_notes: Low-chill variety specifically bred for warm winter areas.

pollinators: Van; Rainier; Stella; Sam; Hartland; Lapins; Sweetheart
disease_notes: Crack-resistant compared to Bing; late bloom reduces frost risk
variety_notes: Heirloom sweet cherry. Dark red heart-shaped fruit. CRITICAL POLLINATION NOTE: Lambert is in the SAME S-allele group (S3S4) as Bing and Royal Ann/Napoleon and CANNOT pollinate them or be pollinated by them. Requires a cross-compatible variety from a DIFFERENT S-allele group, or a self-fertile universal pollinator (Stella or Lapins).
sources: WSU Tree Fruit Extension; One Green World; House Digest; Homesteading.blog; TreeCareZone; Sky Nursery
source_notes: WSU Tree Fruit Extension is authoritative source for sweet cherry S-allele compatibility. The Bing/Lambert incompatibility is the single most important orchard planning fact for this variety.

pollinators: Rainier; Hartland; Lapins; Sam; Stella; Sweetheart; Van; Black Tartarian
disease_notes: Highly prone to rain cracking; susceptible to brown rot in humid climates
variety_notes: The iconic American sweet cherry — dark mahogany-red fruit, large and firm with sweet classic flavor. Originated 1875 in Oregon at the Lewelling farm. CRITICAL: NOT compatible with Lambert, Royal Ann, or Napoleon (same S-allele group). Grows well in dry climates but fruit may crack in wet harvest weather. Universal pollinators like Stella or Lapins are the easiest partners.
sources: Raintree Nursery; Ty Ty Nursery; Gardenia; Leaftide; Smart Garden Experts; Dave Wilson Nursery
source_notes: Chill hours 700-900 per Raintree and Ty Ty. Pollination incompatibilities critically important.

pollinators: Bing; Black Tartarian; Lapins; Van; Hartland; Sam; Stella; Sweetheart
disease_notes: Prone to brown rot in humid climates; problematic in Western Washington
variety_notes: Premium yellow cherry with red blush and cream-to-pale-yellow flesh. Exceptionally sweet (sugar content up to 22 Brix). Released 1952 at WSU by Harold Fogle. Flesh bruises easily — requires careful handling. Birds are less attracted to yellow cherries than red. Ripens just after Bing. Excellent cold hardiness.
sources: Raintree Nursery; Dave Wilson Nursery; Smart Garden Experts; Ty Ty Nursery; Epic Gardening; Gardenia
source_notes: Multiple sources consistent. Not recommended for Western Washington wet climate per Raintree.

disease_notes: Moderately resistant to bacterial canker; does better in wet climates than Bing
variety_notes: The first self-fertile sweet cherry — introduced in 1968 from British Columbia. Revolutionized home cherry growing by eliminating the need for multiple trees. Large dark red heart-shaped fruit with excellent sweet flavor. Also serves as a universal pollinator for other sweet cherries. S-allele genotype S3S4. Sky Nursery chill hours cited as low as 400; Raintree notes uncertainty (400 vs 700-800).
sources: Stark Bros; Raintree Nursery; Gardenia; American Gardener; Ty Ty Nursery; Smart Garden Experts; Leaftide
source_notes: Chill hours range 400-800; low end commonly cited for warmer climates, higher for reliable fruit set in colder zones. Used wider range to reflect both.

disease_notes: Resistant to rain cracking; good disease tolerance
variety_notes: Hybrid of Stella x Van from Summerland Research Station, British Columbia (1983). Self-fertile and serves as a universal pollinator for other sweet cherries. Very large, dark-skinned fruit with firm flesh. Resists cracking in wet weather. Recipient of the Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit. Ripens mid-season with Bing. Holds shape well when baked.
sources: Raintree Nursery; Gardenia; Dave Wilson Nursery; Stark Bros; American Gardener; Specialty Produce
source_notes: Chill hours most commonly cited at 500-700; some sources say 400-500 for low-chill climates.

disease_notes: Low incidence of cracking during summer rains; easier to grow than most cherries
variety_notes: Developed at Summerland Research Station, British Columbia (parentage: Van x Newstar). Self-fertile and also serves as a universal pollinator. Bright red, heart-shaped, medium-to-large fruits with firm aromatic flesh. Very late ripening — about 20 days after Bing. Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit recipient. Precocious (bears fruit young) and heavy yielding. Upright growth.
sources: Raintree Nursery; NatureHills; Stark Bros; Smart Garden Experts; Epic Gardening
source_notes: Chill hours 700-800 per Raintree and NatureHills. Universally praised for ease of growing and crack resistance.

pollinators: Bing; Hartland; Lambert; Lapins; Rainier; Royal Ann; Sam; Stella; Sweetheart
disease_notes: Good disease tolerance; crack-resistant
variety_notes: Released from Summerland Research Station, British Columbia in 1944. Large dark red firm cherry with black-red flesh. Excellent cold hardiness. Ripens slightly before Bing. Often used as a pollination partner for Bing, Rainier, and Lambert because it cross-pollinates with all of them. Heavy bearing tree.
sources: One Green World; Dave Wilson Nursery; Smart Garden Experts; Gardenia
source_notes: Cross-pollination compatibility is excellent — good "utility" pollinator for mixed cherry orchards.

pollinators: Bing; Rainier; Stella; Lapins; Van; Sam; Hartland; Kristen; Sweetheart
disease_notes: Standard sweet cherry disease concerns
variety_notes: Heirloom from Russia, introduced to England in 1796 and to America shortly after. One of the earliest-ripening sweet cherries. Nearly black, richly flavored, purple-fleshed fruit. Well adapted to most soil conditions. CRITICAL: NOT compatible with Lambert, Royal Ann, or Napoleon (same S-allele group as Bing). Used alongside Bing and Rainier in most orchards.
sources: Raintree Nursery; Gardenia; Dave Wilson Nursery; Ty Ty Nursery; Smart Garden Experts; Epic Gardening
source_notes: Chill hours 700+ per Raintree. Early ripening (before Bing) makes it useful for extending the harvest season.

disease_notes: Excellent cold hardiness (to -30F); good disease resistance
variety_notes: THE classic American pie cherry — represents roughly 90% of US sour cherry production. Named for the Montmorency Valley in France. Bright red skin with clear juice and firm yellow flesh. Tart and tangy with balanced acidity. Self-fertile, cold hardy, disease-resistant, and reliable. Tart cherries require fewer chill hours for buds to break but hardier than sweet cherries. Can also pollinate some sweet cherries that bloom at the same time. Ripens before Balaton.
sources: Gardenia; Cummins Nursery; Ison's Nursery; Patuxent Nursery; American Gardener; Ty Ty Nursery; Talbott Nursery
source_notes: Chill hours range 500-1000 across sources; Talbott cites 500, most others 700-1000. Used conservative 700-1000.

disease_notes: Exceptional cold hardiness; tolerates brown rot and leaf spot to a limited extent
variety_notes: Naturally dwarf tart cherry bred by University of Minnesota. Only 8-10 feet tall — perfect for small gardens and container growing. Dark red fruit with mahogany-colored juice. Fruits heavily despite small size. Easy harvest without ladders. Self-fertile and extremely cold-hardy. Bears early (within 3-4 years of planting). Can produce fruit the same year it is planted.
sources: Gardenia; American Gardener; House Digest; Raintree Nursery; Patuxent Nursery
source_notes: Dwarf habit is the standout feature — remains small without dwarfing rootstock.

disease_notes: Susceptible to brown rot and leaf spot; winter-hardiness slightly less than Montmorency
variety_notes: Hungarian variety introduced to North America by Dr. Amy Iezzoni at Michigan State University in the early 1980s. Named for Lake Balaton. Late-blooming (frost-resistant) dark-fleshed Morello-type tart cherry with higher sugar content than Montmorency. Deep burgundy flesh provides vivid pie filling color. Partially self-fertile but yields improve with a sweet cherry pollinator (e.g., Black Gold recommended by Cummins). No bleeding when stem is pulled — crack-resistant.
sources: Cummins Nursery; Gardenia; Patuxent Nursery; American Gardener; House Digest
source_notes: Chill hours not conclusively determined per Cummins; Gardenia suggests 800-1000. Cummins notes partial self-fertility — more nuanced than the typical "self-fertile" label.

disease_notes: Good disease resistance; excellent cold hardiness
variety_notes: Compact semi-dwarf tart cherry from University of Minnesota. About 8 feet wide and tall — great for gardens with limited space. Plump, glistening red fruit. Self-fertile and bears within 2-3 years of planting, faster than Montmorency. Lower chill requirement (450 hours) allows growing as far south as zone 9.
sources: House Digest; Stark Bros; Gardenia
source_notes: Chill hours range widely: House Digest cites 450; other sources up to 800.

disease_notes: Late bloom (reduces frost risk); very cold hardy
variety_notes: Released by Cornell University/Geneva Experiment Station. Bright red fruit with red juice (morello-type). Late-blooming helps avoid spring frosts in marginal cherry-growing areas. Self-fertile and very productive. Firm fruit resists cracking. Good for pies, preserves, and juice.
sources: Cummins Nursery; Stark Bros
source_notes: Less-documented variety; limited but consistent source data.

pollinators: Gala; Fuji; Granny Smith; Golden Delicious; Liberty; Enterprise; McIntosh; Cortland; Haralred; Red Delicious
disease_notes: More susceptible to bitter pit (calcium deficiency) than most varieties — calcium sprays highly recommended; tendency toward biennial bearing
variety_notes: Bred by University of Minnesota in 1974 (released 1991). Exceptionally crisp and juicy with unique cell structure that creates the signature "snap." Late bloomer (bloom group 4) — critical to pair with other late-blooming varieties. Do NOT pair with Cosmic Crisp (too closely related — pollen incompatible). Fruits can split in heavy rain. Sensitive to sunburn. Storage life up to 5-6 months refrigerated.
sources: Stark Bros; Raintree Nursery; Food Forest Nursery; Sunset Magazine; This Old House; Cummins Nursery; Set Apart Farm
source_notes: Chill hours 800-1000 consensus. Late bloom group (4) is the critical orchard-planning fact — some early-blooming varieties like Sunrise are NOT compatible pollinators despite being nearby.

pollinators: Enterprise; Freedom; Honeycrisp; Pristine; Williams Pride; Jonafree; Redfree
disease_notes: Field-immune to apple scab and cedar apple rust; strong resistance to fire blight and powdery mildew — the backbone of any organic orchard
variety_notes: Bred at New York State Agricultural Experiment Station in Geneva (1972 by Dr. Robert Lamb; released 1978). Parentage: Macoun x Purdue 54-12. The name "Liberty" was chosen to denote freedom from disease. Most widely planted disease-resistant apple in the US. Ripens 14 days after McIntosh. Medium-large dark red fruit with crisp nearly-white flesh. Sweet-tart aromatic flavor. Bloom group 2 (early-mid). Narrow harvest window — pick promptly. Stores up to 2 months, flavor improves in first month.
sources: Stark Bros; Cummins Nursery; Missouri Extension; Penn State Extension; Raintree Nursery; Sunset Magazine
source_notes: Zone 4-8 per Cummins; chill hours 800-1000 per Raintree. Universally recommended for organic growers.

pollinators: Liberty; Honeycrisp; Gala; Golden Delicious; GoldRush; Fuji
disease_notes: Immune to apple scab; resistant to fire blight and cedar apple rust; moderately resistant to powdery mildew
variety_notes: Released by PRI (Purdue-Rutgers-Illinois) cooperative breeding program. Medium-large red fruit with tart flesh; peel tends to be tough. Very late ripening (one of the latest). Excellent storage. Highly recommended for disease-resistant orchards where the tough peel is not a drawback. Bloom group 3 (mid-season).
sources: Stark Bros; Missouri Extension; Penn State Extension; Cummins Nursery
source_notes: Universally valued for scab immunity. The tough peel is the main consumer trade-off.

pollinators: Fuji; Granny Smith; Honeycrisp; Golden Delicious; Red Delicious; Empire; Braeburn
disease_notes: Moderately susceptible to apple scab and fire blight; standard pest pressure
variety_notes: New Zealand origin (1934, released 1965). Parentage: Kidd's Orange Red x Golden Delicious. Striped red-over-yellow medium apple, sweet with mild flavor. Kid-friendly. Bears young — good choice for first-time orchardists. Bloom group 3 (mid-season). Late-season bloomer. Widely adaptable mid-range chill. Some sources note partial self-fertility but cross-pollination strongly improves yield.
sources: Food Forest Nursery; Garden Goods Direct; Grow Organic; Raintree Nursery; Stark Bros
source_notes: Chill hours commonly cited at 400-600. Can grow in zones 4-10, but most sources cite 5-9 or 5-10.

pollinators: Gala; Granny Smith; Golden Delicious; Honeycrisp; Braeburn; Cortland; Pristine; Rubinette
disease_notes: Susceptible to fire blight; moderately susceptible to scab
variety_notes: Developed in Aomori Prefecture, Japan (1930s; released 1962). Parentage: Red Delicious x Ralls Janet. Extremely sweet and very crisp — ideal for long storage. Flavor often improves after cool storage. Bloom group 3 (mid-season). Extended bloom period — a good pollinator for many other varieties. Late-season harvest. Low-to-moderate chill requirement makes it well-adapted from zones 5-9. Partially self-fertile in zone 9 but needs pollinator elsewhere.
sources: Garden Goods Direct; NatureHills; Grow Organic; Orange Pippin; Food Forest Nursery
source_notes: Chill hours: NatureHills notes 200-400 for practical purposes, now considered low-chill. Garden Goods Direct cites 350-400. Used 300-500 to span range.

pollinators: Fuji; Gala; Honeycrisp; Golden Delicious; Red Delicious; Rome
disease_notes: Tolerates heat well; moderately susceptible to apple scab and cedar apple rust
variety_notes: Discovered in Australia around 1868 by Maria Ann (Granny) Smith. Iconic bright green tart apple — benchmark baking and pie apple. Firm crisp flesh holds shape when cooked. Long storage life (up to 6 months). Long growing season needed — not suitable for cold northern zones. Bloom group 3 (mid-to-late season). Heat-tolerant. Holds up well during seasonal temperature changes.
sources: Tristar Plants; Raintree Nursery; Grow Organic; Food Forest Nursery; Garden Goods Direct
source_notes: Chill hours: Tristar cites 400-500, others 600+. Range used to reflect.

pollinators: Honeycrisp; Liberty; McIntosh; Empire; Gala; Fuji; Golden Delicious
disease_notes: Susceptible to apple scab; standard pest pressure
variety_notes: Released in 1898 by New York State Agricultural Experiment Station in Geneva. Parentage: Ben Davis x McIntosh. Medium-sized bright red apple with sprightly flavor. Flesh is exceptionally slow to brown when cut — popular for salads and fresh slicing. Excellent all-purpose for eating and cooking. Cold-hardy to zone 3. Bloom group 3 (mid-season). Can serve as a good pollinator for Honeycrisp.
sources: HGTV; Food Forest Nursery; Cummins Nursery; Stark Bros; Grow Organic
source_notes: Cortland is an older heritage variety — extensive documentation.

pollinators: Bosc; Anjou; Moonglow; Seckel (NOT compatible); Harrow Sweet; Comice; Kieffer
disease_notes: Susceptible to fire blight; watch for codling moth
variety_notes: The world's best-selling pear, called Williams in Europe. Discovered in England in 1770. Large golden-yellow bell-shaped fruit with smooth firm flesh and sweet aromatic flavor. Classic canning and fresh-eating pear. Long-lived trees (100+ year bearing). CRITICAL: Bartlett and Seckel CANNOT pollinate each other (incompatibility). Harvest firm and ripen off the tree at room temperature. Partially self-fruitful in western US climates but needs pollinator elsewhere.
sources: Stark Bros; Gardener's Path; Grow Organic; Garden Goods Direct; Set Apart Farm; Dave Wilson Nursery; WSU Tree Fruit Extension
source_notes: Chill hours: Stark Bros says 800, Set Apart Farm says 500-600. Zone range 5-7 or 5-8 or 5-9 depending on source.

pollinators: Bartlett; Anjou; Comice; Moonglow; Seckel; Harrow Sweet
disease_notes: Moderately susceptible to fire blight
variety_notes: Elegant oblong pear with cinnamon-colored russet skin. Distinctive honey-sweet flavor with woodsy spice notes. Firm flesh holds up beautifully in baking and poaching. Keeps up to 3 months in cold storage. Glossy green foliage turns deep purplish burgundy in autumn. Originated in Belgium early 1800s. Late-season ripening.
sources: Stark Bros; Gardener's Path; Grow Organic; Gardens Angle
source_notes: Consistent data across sources.

pollinators: Bartlett; Bosc; Comice; Moonglow; Seckel; Harrow Sweet
disease_notes: Moderately susceptible to fire blight; good scab resistance
variety_notes: Also known as d'Anjou or Beurre d'Anjou. Short-necked egg-shaped fruit with light green skin (sometimes red) and buttery white flesh. Mild sweet flavor. Originated in France mid-1800s. Excellent storage (up to 6 months in cold storage — longest of European pears). Partially self-fertile per WSU but cross-pollination strongly recommended.
sources: Grow Organic; Gardens Angle; Food Gardening Network; WSU Tree Fruit Extension
source_notes: Anjou has the longest cold-storage life of European pears.

pollinators: Bosc; Anjou; Moonglow; Comice; Harrow Sweet; Potomac (NOT compatible); Bartlett (NOT compatible)
disease_notes: Superior fire blight resistance — one of the most disease-resistant pears
variety_notes: American heirloom discovered near Philadelphia in the 18th century (originally by "Dutch Jacob" before being named for landowner Mr. Seckel). Known as the "sugar pear" or "candy pear" — intensely sweet with honeyed depth and subtle spice. Small bite-sized russeted fruit packs more flavor than larger pears. Fine-grained buttery texture. Cold-hardy, frost-resistant. CRITICAL: Seckel and Bartlett CANNOT pollinate each other (same incompatibility group as Potomac). Incompatible with quince rootstock.
sources: Stark Bros; Cummins Nursery; NC State Extension; Gardener's Path
source_notes: Seckel/Bartlett incompatibility and Seckel/Potomac incompatibility both critical orchard facts.

pollinators: Bartlett; Seckel; Bosc; Anjou; Starking Delicious; Harrow Sweet
disease_notes: Excellent fire blight resistance — one of the most resistant European pears
variety_notes: Released by USDA Beltsville Agricultural Research Center, Maryland in 1960. Large yellow-tan fruit with pink blush, resembling Bartlett. Soft juicy melt-in-your-mouth texture with very little grit and mild sweet flavor. Excellent for fresh eating, canning, and juicing. Also an exceptional pollinator for other cultivars due to long-lasting midseason bloom.
sources: Stark Bros; Gurney's; Gardener's Path; The Farm Connection; NC State Extension; UMass Amherst
source_notes: Fire blight resistance makes it especially valuable in humid eastern climates.

pollinators: 20th Century; Hosui; Chojuro; Bartlett
disease_notes: Good fire blight resistance; generally disease-resistant
variety_notes: Name means "new century" in Japanese. Cross between 20th Century and Chojuro. Bright yellow crisp mid-sized fruit. Self-fertile and low-chill — one of the best choices for mild winter climates. Mild flavor and coarse texture. Ripens on the tree (unlike European pears).
sources: Gardener's Path; Garden.org; Four Winds Growers; NatureHills
source_notes: Among the lowest-chill Asian pears — good for zones 8-9.

pollinators: Chojuro; 20th Century; Shinseiki; Shinko; Korean Giant; Bartlett
disease_notes: Better fire blight resistance than many European pears; susceptible to bacterial canker
variety_notes: Name means "abundant juice" or "much water" in Japanese. Consistently rated the best-tasting Asian pear at Dave Wilson Nursery tastings. Large brownish-orange russeted fruit with juicy sweet fine-grained white flesh. 12% sugar content. Balanced sweet-tangy flavor (slightly higher acid than other Asian pears). Vigorous tree with loose spreading growth habit. More tart in cool-climate / short-summer areas.
sources: Stark Bros; Gardener's Path; One Green World; C&J Gardening Center; Legg Creek Farm; UC ANR
source_notes: Fire blight susceptibility noted by UC ANR — not as clean as some sources suggest. Chill hours vary widely 300-700.

pollinators: Hosui; 20th Century; Shinseiki; Bartlett; Anjou
disease_notes: Moderate fire blight susceptibility
variety_notes: Traditional Japanese variety. Firm gold-to-russet fruit with distinctive sweet butterscotch flavor. Stores up to 5 months. Round upright growth form. Good home-garden scale. Note: UC ANR considers Chojuro inferior quality vs newer varieties, but Gardener's Path rates it a home garden favorite.
sources: Gardener's Path; NatureHills; Legg Creek Farm; UC ANR
source_notes: Quality assessments vary — commercial orchard sources now consider it dated, but home gardeners still value it for unique flavor.

pollinators: Shinseiki; Hosui; Chojuro; Bartlett
disease_notes: Good fire blight resistance; susceptible to codling moth
variety_notes: Also known as Nijisseiki — Japanese for "Twentieth Century." Golden-yellow fruit with rosy blush. Crisp apple-like texture with mild sweet flavor. Abundant, productive bearer requiring heavy thinning. Self-fertile but much larger crops with pollinator. Does NOT cross-pollinate effectively with European pears. Excellent cold hardiness (protect when temps fall below -20F). Pyramidal tree shape. Vibrant orange-red fall foliage. Ranks among most popular Asian pears in US.
sources: Gardener's Path; Four Winds Growers; NatureHills; Garden.org; UC ANR
source_notes: One of the most widely planted Asian pears in North America.

pollinators: Hosui; Chojuro; 20th Century; Shinseiki; Korean Giant
disease_notes: Good fire blight resistance (one of the best among Asian pears)
variety_notes: Medium-large russet-skinned fruit with crisp white flesh and rich sweet flavor — often rated among best-flavored Asian pears especially in hot climates. Productive tree requires heavy thinning. Keeps 2-3 months in cold storage. Particularly valued for fire blight resistance — does well in humid eastern climates where other Asian pears struggle.
sources: Garden.org; UC ANR; Four Winds Growers
source_notes: Garden.org author reports superior performance in zone 8 heavy clay compared to Hosui.

pollinators: Italian Prune; Mount Royal; Green Gage; Damson; Brooks
disease_notes: Resistant to black knot and bacterial spot; good disease resistance overall
variety_notes: Licensed by Cornell University; introduced in 1926. THE standard European prune plum. Medium-large oval dark blue freestone fruit with yellow-green flesh. Excellent for fresh eating, drying (can be dried without pitting due to freestone habit), canning, and preserves. Blooms later than most plums — less susceptible to late frost. Self-fertile but heavier yields with a partner. Good for humid climates except where black knot is severe.
sources: Stark Bros; Gardenia; Raintree Nursery; Gurney's; Minneopa Orchards; Plant Me Green; Fruits and Shoots; Trees of Antiquity
source_notes: Chill hours 700-800 across sources. Zone range most commonly 5-7 per Stark Bros; 4-8 per Gardenia and Fruits and Shoots.

pollinators: Stanley; Green Gage; Mount Royal; Brooks (bloom overlap is poor — self-pollination is typical)
disease_notes: Generally disease-resistant; standard plum pest pressure
variety_notes: Also called Fellenberg. Large dark purple-blue oval freestone fruit with yellowish-green flesh. Sweet rich flavor. One of the best European prune plums for drying — made into prunes commercially in Pacific Northwest. Blooms very late — poor pollination overlap with other plums means typically self-pollinated. Very productive once established.
sources: Raintree Nursery; Stark Bros; Tree Care Zone
source_notes: Late bloom is a defining characteristic — "blooms so late there is poor pollination overlap with other plums" per Raintree.

pollinators: Stanley; Italian Prune; Mount Royal; Damson
disease_notes: Can be susceptible to black knot in humid climates
variety_notes: Ancient French heirloom (known as Reine Claude), named for Sir William Gage who introduced it to England from France in 1725. Round medium-sized greenish-yellow fruit with amber-colored flesh. Considered one of the finest-flavored plums — exceptionally sweet with honey-like depth. Classic dessert plum.
sources: Stark Bros; Trees of Antiquity; Cummins Nursery
source_notes: Heirloom variety — extensively documented but chill hours inconsistent across sources.

disease_notes: Excellent disease resistance; cold hardy; reliable
variety_notes: Ancient species (Prunus insititia) distinct from typical European plums (Prunus domestica). Small oval dark blue-purple fruit with tart astringent flavor — not for fresh eating, but transforms beautifully into jams, preserves, and damson gin. Extremely reliable, cold hardy, disease-resistant. Self-fertile — no pollinator needed. Often the toughest plum for marginal climates.
sources: Stark Bros; Cummins Nursery
source_notes: A distinct species (P. insititia) rather than a cultivar of P. domestica. Primarily a cooking/preserving plum.

pollinators: Stanley; Italian Prune; Green Gage
disease_notes: Very cold hardy; good disease resistance
variety_notes: Canadian origin (Montreal, Quebec) — bred for cold hardiness. Medium-sized dark blue oval fruit with yellow-green flesh. Sweet flavor ideal for fresh eating, canning, and preserves. Freestone. Good companion pollinator for Stanley. Cold-hardy to zone 4.
sources: Stark Bros; Minneopa Orchards
source_notes: Bred for cold hardiness — key feature is zone 4 reliability.

pollinators: Burbank; Shiro; Satsuma; Methley; Elephant Heart; Ozark Premier
disease_notes: Susceptible to bacterial spot; somewhat resistant to black knot
variety_notes: Bred by Luther Burbank in Santa Rosa, California and introduced in 1906. Long considered the industry standard for Japanese plum flavor. Medium-sized round fruit with purplish-red skin speckled with pale dots. Yellow flesh near pit, deep red near skin. Rich aromatic flavor. Self-fertile and considered a "universal pollenizer" for Japanese and hybrid plums. Low chill makes it adaptable from Michigan to Texas. Tolerates cold down to -10F.
sources: Fast Growing Trees; Stark Bros; Cummins Nursery; Chestnut Hill Nursery; Minneopa Orchards; Tree Care Zone
source_notes: Chill hours vary from 300 (Fast Growing Trees, Stark Bros) to 700 (Cummins Nursery). Most home-orchard sources cite the lower number; commercial sources higher.

pollinators: Santa Rosa; Methley; Burbank; Ozark Premier; Beauty
disease_notes: Moderate disease resistance
variety_notes: Bred by Luther Burbank around 1899. "Shiro" is Japanese for white. Yellow-skinned medium-sized round fruit with juicy amber flesh. Sweet mild flavor. Very heavy producer — requires thinning. Early-ripening (July) — good for extending plum harvest at the beginning. Not self-fertile — requires Japanese plum pollinator.
sources: Stark Bros; Cummins Nursery; NatureHills
source_notes: Consistent data across sources.

pollinators: Santa Rosa; Shiro; Burbank; Beauty
disease_notes: Very winter hardy and disease resistant
variety_notes: Believed to be a Japanese-American hybrid, discovered as a chance seedling in South Africa in the early 1920s. Beloved by home growers since. Red-purple clingstone fruit with deep crimson juicy flesh. Mild sweet flavor. LOWEST CHILL requirement of all plums — only 150 hours needed. Blooms late which helps avoid spring frosts despite low chill. Self-fertile and blooms heavily attracting pollinators.
sources: Raintree Nursery; Stark Bros; NatureHills; Tree Care Zone
source_notes: Raintree notes "Lowest chill of all plums - only 150 hours."

pollinators: Santa Rosa; Shiro; Methley; Burbank
disease_notes: Moderate disease resistance; standard plum pest pressure
variety_notes: Bred at the University of Missouri, introduced in 1946. Extra-large (up to 3 inches) red-blushed pink-skinned fruit with yellow flesh — among the largest of Japanese plums. Sweet juicy flavor. Good pollinator partner for Santa Rosa and Methley. Requires cross-pollination.
sources: Stark Bros
source_notes: Less documented than Santa Rosa but solid data from primary source.

pollinators: Santa Rosa; Superior; Pipestone; Waneta; Methley
disease_notes: Excellent cold hardiness; good disease resistance; reliable in cold climates
variety_notes: Also known as Bubblegum plum due to distinctive bubblegum-like flavor. Cold-hardy hybrid (Japanese x American plum) bred by N.E. Hansen at South Dakota State University in 1911. Medium-sized red-skinned fruit with yellow flesh. Reliable fruit set in zone 3-4 where most plums fail. Good pollinator for other American and American hybrid plums. Requires cross-pollination.
sources: Stark Bros; Cummins Nursery
source_notes: Cold-hardy hybrid species crosses — essential for zone 3-4 growers.

disease_notes: Susceptible to bacterial canker in wet climates; spray copper preventatively
variety_notes: Heirloom from England late 1600s, mentioned in Jane Austen's Mansfield Park (1814). Large 2-2.5 inch golden-orange fruit with red blush; freestone. Very early bloomer — requires frost protection in zones 5-6. Blooms in April. Self-fertile but yields improve with second apricot nearby.
sources: Stark Bros; One Green World; Planting Justice; J. Frank Schmidt; Gardenia; NatureHills; Trees of Antiquity
source_notes: Height varies widely across sources (10-30 ft); used 10-15 ft as the consistent middle. Diggers Club (AU) lists 350 chill hours but that conflicts with 5 US sources at 600-700.

disease_notes: Good disease resistance; less susceptible to bacterial canker than some apricots
variety_notes: Classic California commercial apricot, popular since the 1890s. Medium-large golden-yellow fruit with red blush. Sweet rich flavor. Freestone. Excellent for canning, drying, and fresh eating. Self-fertile. Good pollinator for Moorpark.
sources: Dave Wilson Nursery; Stark Bros
source_notes: Long-established commercial variety.

disease_notes: Resistant to bacterial spot, brown rot, and perennial canker — among the most disease-resistant apricots
variety_notes: Developed at Harrow Research Station in Ontario, Canada. Late bloomer — avoids frost damage better than most apricots. Large orange-pink fruit with juicy rich flavor. Freestone. Self-fertile. Excellent cold hardiness. Outstanding disease resistance makes it ideal for humid eastern climates.
sources: Stark Bros; Cummins Nursery; One Green World
source_notes: Harrow breeding program focus on disease resistance shows in this variety.

disease_notes: Excellent cold hardiness and bud hardiness; some disease resistance
variety_notes: Released by Michigan State University in 1967. Medium-large golden-yellow freestone fruit. Late bloom makes it frost-resistant. Specifically bred for cold climates — one of the best apricots for zone 4. Sweet flavor. Self-fertile and vigorous grower.
sources: Stark Bros
source_notes: Less commonly sold but well-documented at Stark Bros.

disease_notes: Better than average tolerance to bacterial canker and brown rot; adapted to wet climates
variety_notes: Released by Washington State University in 1953. Medium-sized orange-red fruit with excellent flavor. Specifically selected for Puget Sound maritime climate — tolerates wet springs and cool summers better than most apricots. Self-fertile. Ideal for Pacific Northwest.
sources: Raintree Nursery; One Green World
source_notes: Niche variety bred for Pacific Northwest conditions — essential for maritime growers.

disease_notes: Excellent disease and pest resistance; few insect problems
variety_notes: Also called Bensonhurst Purple. The most cold-hardy fig available. Stems hardy to 10F; roots survive to -20F. In zone 5-6, stems may die back to ground in winter but will regrow from roots and produce fruit on new wood. Zone 5 with heavy mulch and protection. Purple-skinned medium fruit with sweet strawberry-pink flesh. Self-fertile common fig — no pollinator wasp required.
sources: Gardener's Path; The Fig Father; Online Fig Trees; Henderson Garden Supply; TreeVitalize
source_notes: Best choice for zone 5-6 in-ground growing. Will die back in cold winters but reliably regrows.

disease_notes: Shallow, somewhat invasive roots; otherwise disease-resistant
variety_notes: The most adaptable and widely-grown fig in the US. Cold-hardy to 10F — hardy in zone 7-9, overwinters in zone 6 with protection. Often produces two crops per year (breba + main). Bronze-purple fruit with mild sweet honey-like flavor. Self-fertile common fig. Forgiving of varied conditions. Can be pruned into bonsai or kept small in containers. Multiple varieties share this name (California Brown Turkey vs English Brown Turkey).
sources: Henderson Garden Supply; Gardener's Path; Gardening Know How; Silver Run Forest Farm; PlantingTree
source_notes: Be aware that "Brown Turkey" refers to multiple different cultivars — California Brown Turkey and English Brown Turkey are distinct.

disease_notes: Closed-eye fruit ("bee-less" type) resists souring and pest entry — especially valuable in humid climates
variety_notes: Also called Celestial or "Sugar Fig" — cherished since the 1600s. Hardy down to 5-10F — slightly more cold-hardy than Brown Turkey. Recovers quickly from winter dieback. Rosy-purple to light purple-brown medium fruit with intensely sweet honey flavor. THE best fig for humid Deep South — closed eye prevents souring and pest damage in wet heat. Popular in Louisiana. Self-fertile common fig.
sources: Gardener's Path; Online Fig Trees; The Fig Father; Silver Run Forest Farm; TreeVitalize; Gardening Know How
source_notes: Closed-eye (bee-less) structure is the defining feature — essential for humid southern growers.

disease_notes: Good disease resistance; thrives in dry Mediterranean-like climates
variety_notes: Classic warm-climate fig — the iconic California commercial variety. Less cold-hardy than Chicago Hardy or Brown Turkey (zone 7+). Large tree habit — can reach 30 feet unpruned. Deep purple-black skin with rich strawberry-red interior. Honey-sweet jammy intense flavor — rated best-tasting by many. Self-fertile common fig. Two crops per year.
sources: Henderson Garden Supply; Gardener's Path; The Fig Father
source_notes: Best suited to zone 7+ climates. Richer flavor than Chicago Hardy but less cold-hardy.

disease_notes: Good general disease resistance
variety_notes: Yellow-green "honey fig" — lighter colored skin with amber cream flesh. Excellent for drying and canning (commercially grown for canning). Flavor shines when dried; texture becomes spreadable like jam when cooked. Low chill requirement. Needs sunshine and dry soil. Self-fertile common fig.
sources: Silver Run Forest Farm
source_notes: Primarily a commercial canning fig; also grown by home gardeners in zone 7+.

disease_notes: Excellent cold hardiness and reliable production in cool-summer climates
variety_notes: THE best fig for the Pacific Northwest and other cool-summer maritime climates. Reliably ripens its breba (first) crop even where other figs fail. Medium-large green-skinned fruit with strawberry-red flesh. Sweet rich flavor. Main crop typically doesn't mature in cool climates but breba crop alone is generous. Self-fertile common fig.
sources: Raintree Nursery; One Green World
source_notes: Niche but essential variety for Pacific NW growers.

pollinators: Shenandoah; Susquehanna; Mango; Overleese; NC-1
disease_notes: Less resistant to phyllosticta spot than other pawpaws; otherwise pest and disease free
variety_notes: Selected from the wild in Chanute, Kansas (1970). One of the older named varieties. Often cited as self-fertile though this is debated by expert growers. Large fruit with yellow flesh. Can have a bitter aftertaste in some fruit depending on the year. Low acetogenin content. Falling out of favor with newer improved varieties but still widely planted. Pawpaws need 2200 Growing Degree Days to ripen fruit.
sources: Cultivar.guide; Raintree Nursery; Clemson HGIC
source_notes: "Self-fertile" claim is questionable per Cultivar.guide — most growers still recommend cross-pollination.

pollinators: Susquehanna; Sunflower; NC-1; Mango; Potomac
disease_notes: No significant disease or pest problems; naturally resistant
variety_notes: Patented variety developed by Neal Peterson in Boyce, Virginia (patented 2004). Among the best-flavored and largest pawpaws — individual fruits weigh up to 1 lb. Sweet, flavorful, creamy-yellow custard-like flesh. Mild flavor — important quality since pawpaws are naturally rich and intense. Medium to large yellow fruit with few seeds. Zone 5-8 hardy to -20F. Flowers self-incompatible — requires genetically different pollinator.
sources: Raintree Nursery; NC State Extension; One Green World; Planting Justice
source_notes: Peterson Pawpaw releases are the gold standard — Shenandoah specifically bred for mild flavor.

pollinators: Shenandoah; Sunflower; NC-1; Mango; Potomac
disease_notes: Some reports of delayed graft failure or other shortened-lifespan issues
variety_notes: Patented variety by Neal Peterson (2004). Largest fruit of Peterson's collection — over 1 lb. Firmer than ripe avocado (firmer than most pawpaws). Stronger flavor than Shenandoah. Low seed ratio — only 3-6% seed. Late-ripening. Medium yields (~40 fruits per mature tree). Thick skin resists damage.
sources: Raintree Nursery; NC State Extension; Cultivar.guide; Planting Justice
source_notes: Tree lifespan concerns noted in some reports per Cultivar.guide — worth flagging.

pollinators: Shenandoah; Sunflower; Susquehanna; NC-1
disease_notes: Pest and disease free
variety_notes: Selection from Georgia. Fast-growing variety with large sweet orange-fleshed fruit. Tropical mango-like flavor. Heavier producer than some Peterson varieties. Zones 5-9.
sources: Planting Justice; One Green World
source_notes: Southern pawpaw selection — good for warmer parts of the pawpaw range.

pollinators: Shenandoah; Sunflower; Susquehanna; Mango
disease_notes: Disease and pest resistant
variety_notes: Selected in West Virginia by Homer Jacobs in 1934. Compact and hardy tree. Good crops of large, very sweet, orange-yellow fruit. One of the older heirloom pawpaw selections.
sources: Planting Justice
source_notes: Well-established heirloom variety.

disease_notes: Pest resistant; scale insects and aphids occasional; fungal leaf spot in humid climates
variety_notes: Also called Apple Persimmon. The world's most popular persimmon — outsells other major fruits. NON-ASTRINGENT — can be eaten while still firm and crisp like an apple. Flat tomato-shaped fruit. Self-fertile; sets parthenocarpic (seedless) fruit when grown alone. Honey-sweet flavor with mango notes. Gorgeous orange fall fruit persists on tree. Long-lived (50-75 years). Low chill requirement.
sources: NatureHills; Food Forest Nursery; Already Smart Gardening; UC ANR; A Natural Farm; Grow Organic
source_notes: Self-fertile with seedless fruit is a signature feature — but will produce seeded fruit if another persimmon is nearby.

disease_notes: Generally pest and disease free
variety_notes: The variety most often found in stores. 4-inch acorn/cone-shaped fruit, deep orange when ripe. Very sweet and flavorful when fully ripe — sweeter than non-astringent Fuyu. ASTRINGENT — MUST be eaten when fully soft-ripe (like pudding consistency) or it will pucker the mouth. Great dried. Late to ripen — best in long hot growing season. Striking fall color. Can be frozen then thawed to mimic ripening.
sources: Raintree Nursery; Stark Bros; UC ANR; Grow Organic
source_notes: Astringency when unripe is CRITICAL — significantly affects consumer experience and timing.

pollinators: other American persimmon seedlings (many American persimmons are dioecious — need male and female trees)
disease_notes: Very pest and disease resistant; hardy native species
variety_notes: Native American persimmon (Diospyros virginiana) — very different from Asian kaki persimmons. Much more cold-hardy (zone 4-9 vs 7-10 for Asian). Small round golden-orange fruit about 1-2 inches — much smaller than Asian. VERY astringent until fully ripe after frost — tradition says "not ripe until after frost." Trees typically dioecious (separate male and female trees) but some self-fertile cultivars exist (e.g., Meader). Can reach 30-60 feet in ideal conditions.
sources: Grow Organic; Gardenia
source_notes: Chill hours essentially zero (technically not applicable) because native species — set to 0 in schema. "Not ripe until after frost" is a critical home-growing fact.

disease_notes: Pest and disease resistant
variety_notes: Self-fertile American persimmon developed by Professor Meader at University of New Hampshire. Seedless fruits when grown alone. Reliable bearer even in marginal climates. About 2 inches in diameter. Astringent until fully soft-ripe. More manageable size than wild American persimmons. Excellent for northern growers who want persimmons but can't grow Asian types.
sources: One Green World; Raintree Nursery
source_notes: Meader is the go-to self-fertile American persimmon for home growers in zones 4-6.

disease_notes: Hardy hybrid vigor; pest and disease resistant
variety_notes: Hybrid of American x Asian persimmon developed at Nikitsky Botanical Garden in Crimea. Bridges the gap between the two species: Asian-quality large fruit (2-3 inch) with American cold-hardiness (hardy to zone 5). Astringent variety — must fully ripen. Excellent flavor. Self-fertile.
sources: One Green World; Raintree Nursery
source_notes: Increasingly popular as a way to grow quality persimmons in cooler zones.

disease_notes: Pest and disease resistant; very hardy
variety_notes: Classic American hybrid (white x red mulberry). Extended fruiting season — bears over 2-3 months rather than one flush. Large sweet dark purple-black fruit with excellent flavor. Self-fertile. Cold-hardy to zone 4 — hardiest named mulberry variety. Bears very young (often in year 2). Birds LOVE these. Plant intentionally as bird-distraction crop for other fruit trees.
sources: One Green World; Stark Bros; Raintree Nursery
source_notes: Long fruiting season is the defining feature.

disease_notes: Generally pest and disease resistant
variety_notes: Exceptional-flavored mulberry from Pakistan. Extraordinarily long dark red to nearly black fruit — up to 3-5 inches long (twice the length of most mulberries). Rich complex sweet-tart flavor — considered among the best-flavored mulberries. Less cold hardy than Illinois Everbearing (zone 7+). Self-fertile.
sources: One Green World; Raintree Nursery
source_notes: Exceptional fruit size and flavor — but warm-climate only.

disease_notes: Pest and disease resistant
variety_notes: Serbian variety with large black highly-flavored fruit. Sweet-tart with rich flavor. Self-fertile. Productive. Somewhat more cold-hardy than Pakistan.
sources: One Green World; Raintree Nursery
source_notes: Less commonly grown than Illinois Everbearing or Pakistan but worth noting.

disease_notes: Excellent disease resistance; long-lived
variety_notes: True Persian/black mulberry (Morus nigra) — a different species from most American mulberries (M. alba, M. rubra, hybrids). Large dark purple-black fruit with intensely rich complex flavor — considered by many to be the finest-flavored mulberry. Long-lived trees (centuries in favorable climates). Self-fertile. Zone 6+ and prefers milder climates. Slow to bear (3-5 years) but worth the wait.
sources: One Green World; Raintree Nursery
source_notes: Genuine Morus nigra — distinguish from other species marketed as "black mulberry."

disease_notes: Moderate disease resistance; generally hardy
variety_notes: THE iconic commercial pomegranate variety — accounts for most US production. Large red fruit with deep red arils and sweet-tart juicy flavor. Self-fertile shrub/small tree. Long-lived (can live 200+ years). Requires hot summers to ripen fruit properly. Zone 7+ with cold protection; reliably productive zone 8+.
sources: Stark Bros; Raintree Nursery; One Green World
source_notes: The default commercial pomegranate.

disease_notes: Cold-hardy; one of the most disease-resistant pomegranates
variety_notes: Russian heirloom from the Caucasus — one of the most cold-hardy pomegranates (zone 6 with protection). Large fruit with deep red arils. Sweet-tart flavor. Self-fertile. Good choice for marginal pomegranate climates.
sources: One Green World; Raintree Nursery
source_notes: Cold-hardy pomegranate for growers pushing zone 6.

disease_notes: Standard pomegranate pest/disease concerns
variety_notes: Sweeter, less acidic alternative to Wonderful. Pink-to-red arils with mild sweet flavor — good for fresh eating straight from the fruit rather than juicing. Ripens earlier than Wonderful. Self-fertile.
sources: Raintree Nursery; One Green World
source_notes: Named "Sweet" literally for its flavor profile vs tarter varieties.

disease_notes: Good disease resistance
variety_notes: Russian heirloom considered the best-flavored pomegranate by many connoisseurs. Balanced sweet-tart flavor with berry notes. Small soft edible seeds (can eat whole — no spitting). Red arils in pink-red fruit. Self-fertile. Testing grounds at UC Davis consistently rate it among top flavor.
sources: One Green World; Raintree Nursery
source_notes: Increasingly popular with home growers for flavor and soft seeds.

pollinators: Theta; Yamhill; Eta; Santiam (must be compatible pollinizer, not all hazelnuts cross-pollinate)
disease_notes: Resistant to Eastern Filbert Blight (EFB) — a major advance over older varieties
variety_notes: Released by Oregon State University in 2009. EFB-RESISTANT — critical because Eastern Filbert Blight has historically devastated hazelnut plantings outside the Pacific Northwest. Large round kernels with excellent flavor. The best modern hazelnut variety for most of the US. NOT self-fertile — requires EFB-resistant pollinizer (Theta, Yamhill, Eta, Santiam — NOT older susceptible varieties).
sources: One Green World; Raintree Nursery; OSU Extension
source_notes: EFB resistance is the critical orchard-planning fact for hazelnuts.

pollinators: Jefferson; Yamhill; Eta; Dorris
disease_notes: EFB-resistant — Oregon State University release
variety_notes: Bred at Oregon State University as an EFB-resistant pollinizer for Jefferson. Produces good quality nuts as well. Late-season. Essential partner variety in EFB-resistant hazelnut orchards.
sources: One Green World; OSU Extension
source_notes: Primarily planted as pollinizer for Jefferson.

pollinators: Jefferson; Theta; Eta
disease_notes: Highly EFB-resistant — Oregon State release
variety_notes: Released by OSU in 2008. Excellent EFB resistance. Medium-sized round nuts with good flavor. Early ripening. Productive. Good pollinizer for Jefferson. Smaller stature makes it suitable for smaller plantings.
sources: One Green World; OSU Extension
source_notes: Early-bearing EFB-resistant variety.

pollinators: Jefferson; Theta; Yamhill
disease_notes: EFB-resistant — OSU release
variety_notes: EFB-resistant pollinizer released by OSU. Primarily planted as pollinator partner for other EFB-resistant varieties. Produces small but flavorful nuts. Late-season bloomer.
sources: One Green World; OSU Extension
source_notes: Pollinizer-focused variety.

pollinators: Kanza; Lakota; Mohawk (Type II pollinizers needed — Pawnee is Type I protandrous)
disease_notes: Good scab resistance; moderate disease resistance overall
variety_notes: USDA release (1984). Early-ripening pecan — an advantage in northern growing areas where frost may hit late crops. Medium-large oval nuts with excellent flavor. Type I (protandrous) — sheds pollen before receiving it, so pollinated by Type II variety. Productive. Becoming one of the most widely-planted pecan varieties.
sources: Stark Bros; One Green World; Texas Pecan Nursery
source_notes: Protandrous/protogynous (Type I/Type II) distinction is critical for pecan orchard planning.

pollinators: Pawnee; Lakota (Type I pollinizers needed — Kanza is Type II protogynous)
disease_notes: Excellent scab resistance — one of the most disease-resistant pecans
variety_notes: USDA release (1996). Type II (protogynous). Excellent scab resistance — essential for humid climates. Small-medium nuts but high quality and heavy production. Cold-hardy — one of the best pecans for northern growers (zone 5). Pairs beautifully with Pawnee (Type I).
sources: Stark Bros; One Green World; Texas Pecan Nursery; UGA Extension
source_notes: Best-in-class scab resistance makes it top choice for wet southern climates.

pollinators: Pawnee (Type I pollinizers — Lakota is Type II protogynous)
disease_notes: Excellent scab resistance and good general disease resistance
variety_notes: USDA release (2007). Type II (protogynous). Large thin-shelled nuts with high-quality kernels. Excellent scab resistance. Heavy annual production without alternate bearing issues. Good pairing with Pawnee.
sources: Texas Pecan Nursery; Stark Bros
source_notes: Newer release — excellent commercial characteristics.

pollinators: Desirable; Pawnee (Type I pollinizers — Stuart is Type II protogynous)
disease_notes: Moderate scab resistance; susceptible in humid southern climates
variety_notes: Classic older pecan variety (1893) — historically the most widely planted commercial pecan. Large thick-shelled nuts with dark kernels. Type II. Slow to bear (6-10 years). Long-lived and productive once established. Tendency toward alternate bearing. Less disease-resistant than newer varieties but still valued as a heritage cultivar.
sources: Stark Bros; Texas Pecan Nursery; UGA Extension
source_notes: Older variety — newer releases have better disease resistance but Stuart is a heritage benchmark.

pollinators: Pawnee; Kanza (Type I pollinizers — Mohawk is Type II protogynous)
disease_notes: Moderate scab susceptibility
variety_notes: USDA release (1965). Type II. Large nuts with high kernel percentage. Moderate scab susceptibility — better suited to drier climates (OK; TX; NM) than humid southeast.
sources: Stark Bros; Texas Pecan Nursery
source_notes: Older commercial variety with large nut size.
